raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to mitigate the lead-related complications associated with traditional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs). Transvenous systems are associated with acute risks such as pneumothorax and cardiac perforation, as well as long-term vulnerabilities including lead fracture, venous obstruction, and systemic intravascular infection [1]. By utilizing an entirely extra-thoracic design, the S-ICD eliminates the need for transvenous lead placement, thereby sparing the vasculature and cardiac structures [2]. Early feasibility and safety were demonstrated in seminal regulatory studies, establishing the S-ICD as a viable alternative for patients at risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD) who do not require pacing [3]. Subsequent real-world registries, such as the EFFORTLESS registry, confirmed the high efficacy of shock therapy in terminating ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF) [4, 5].

Rigorous clinical evaluation has established the S-ICD as a frontline therapy. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial, a multicenter randomized controlled trial, demonstrated that the S-ICD is non-inferior to the TV-ICD concerning the composite primary endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [6]. Additionally, the prospective UNTOUCHED trial highlighted that modern device programming and the use of high-rate detection zones significantly lower inappropriate shock rates in primary prevention patients with a low ejection fraction [7]. Real-world post-approval registries have consistently mirrored these clinical trial findings, demonstrating excellent shock conversion rates and low long-term complication rates [8]. Long-term five-year outcomes from the EFFORTLESS registry confirmed that the clinical benefits of the S-ICD are sustained over time, with low device-related infection rates and minimal system failure [9]. Systematic analyses and propensity-matched studies comparing S-ICD to TV-ICD cohorts have reinforced these findings, showing equivalent mortality outcomes and similar overall safety profiles [10, 11]. Moreover, patient-reported outcomes indicate that quality of life is maintained or even improved following S-ICD implantation when compared to transvenous alternatives [12].

Despite these advantages, careful patient selection remains paramount. According to current consensus statements and clinical guidelines, the S-ICD is recommended for patients who have an indication for an ICD but do not require pacing for bradycardia, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) [13, 14, 15]. To minimize the risk of inappropriate shocks caused by cardiac oversensing—such as T-wave oversensing or myopotentials—candidates must undergo mandatory pre-implantation electrocardiographic (ECG) screening [16]. This screening involves evaluating surface ECG complexes across three prospective sensing vectors in both supine and standing positions [17]. Utilizing either manual or automated screening tools, clinicians verify that the patient has at least one suitable vector to prevent oversensing [18]. Recent real-world validations of automated screening algorithms have demonstrated high specificity and sensitivity in predicting successful post-implantation sensing [19].

The surgical implantation of the S-ICD has also evolved to optimize safety and patient comfort. The procedure consists of creating a lateral thoracic generator pocket and positioning a subcutaneous lead parallel to the left sternal border [20]. While early procedures relied on a three-incision technique, a simplified two-incision approach has become widely adopted, reducing operative time and minimizing surgical wounds without compromising safety [21, 22]. Furthermore, pocket placement has shifted from a subcutaneous location to an intermuscular position between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles [23]. This intermuscular technique provides superior cosmetic outcomes, reduces the risk of device erosion, and lowers shock thresholds by optimizing the defibrillation vector [24]. S-ICD therapy has also proven highly feasible and safe in pediatric patients and individuals with congenital heart disease, where vascular access is frequently compromised [25].

A historical challenge of S-ICD therapy was the occurrence of inappropriate shocks, primarily triggered by T-wave oversensing [16]. However, technological innovations have drastically mitigated this issue. The development of advanced signal processing software, notably the SMART Pass filter, has substantially reduced inappropriate therapies by filtering out low-frequency signals typical of T-waves while preserving high-frequency R-wave sensing [26]. Clinical studies have confirmed that enabling this filter reduces inappropriate shock rates by up to 70% without delaying VF detection [27].

The primary limitation of the S-ICD remains its inability to deliver bradycardia pacing or ATP. To overcome this, modular cardiac rhythm management systems are currently being developed. Feasibility trials have successfully demonstrated wireless, bidirectional communication between an S-ICD and a leadless pacemaker (LCP) [28]. In this modular setup, the S-ICD detects VT/VF and can trigger the LCP to deliver ATP, potentially terminating tachyarrhythmias without the need for a painful high-voltage shock [29]. This combination provides a completely extra-vascular solution for patients who require pacing capabilities [30]. In conclusion, the S-ICD is a robust, safe, and effective therapy for preventing sudden cardiac death, with evolving software and modular technologies continuously expanding its clinical utility.
